conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use a short, well-studied tool called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply 10 questions about the past week, and your answers are completely confidential. We’ll go at your pace; there are no right or wrong responses, and my only goal is to understand how I can best support you. Ready to start?

1. In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when small everyday frustrations pop up?

Oh—yeah, I guess I still laugh. Maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my husband makes a silly joke or when the dog does something goofy, I’ll chuckle. So… most of the time, just not every single second.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time, I can still laugh—maybe not quite as quickly as before, but yeah, I do find things funny and catch myself smiling at little stuff the baby does or when my husband cracks a joke.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller when it’s sunny. I don’t jump out of bed excited or anything, but I do have little things I enjoy planning.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her, I might think “ugh, should’ve waited,” but I don’t dwell on it. I figure babies are messy and I’m doing my best, so I let it go pretty quickly.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah—like I’ll suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay in the middle of the night, even though the monitor looks fine. It’s not every minute, and it’s not super intense, but those little worries do pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden panic. A couple of times I’ve felt a quick flutter of worry—mostly when I hear an odd noise on the monitor—but it’s gone as soon as I check on her. Nothing that feels like a real scare.
Things have been getting on top of me
Not really—some days the laundry or dishes pile up, but I just tackle them when I can. I feel like I’m keeping up overall, no big “drowning” feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay. Once I’m out, I stay out—unless the baby wakes me, of course. I don’t lie there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of teary moments—mostly when I’m extra tired—but it passes quickly. Overall I wouldn’t call myself sad or miserable; just normal new-mom ups and downs.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had that kind of crying. Maybe a single quick tear when I was overtired last week, but not real sobbing or anything like that.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You're doing a beautiful job adjusting to new motherhood. You shared that you're still able to laugh and look forward to small pleasures like coffee or stroller walks, even if your enthusiasm is a notch quieter than before. Occasional <sym>worry</sym> about your baby's breathing pops up at night, and you've felt briefly teary when tired, yet these moments pass quickly and you feel generally on top of daily tasks. Most importantly, you denied feeling overwhelmed, persistently low, or having any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 6, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes sudden, unprovoked worries about baby's breathing that occur "sometimes" without external trigger, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 6 falls well below the 9-point threshold where <med>postpartum depression</med> becomes possible. You endorse only mild, transient <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>sadness</sym> that do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which requires five or more symptoms (including either depressed mood or loss of interest) for two weeks, plus clinically significant distress or impairment. Your preserved sleep when the baby sleeps, intact enjoyment of activities, and absence of guilt, panic, or self-harm thoughts further support a low-risk picture. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum check-ups and re-screen with EPDS at 4-6 weeks or sooner if mood or anxiety worsens
2. Practice good sleep hygiene: nap when baby naps, limit screen time before bed, and accept help with night feeds when possible
3. Try brief relaxation techniques (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) when nocturnal worries arise
4. Share any escalating <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, or thoughts of self-harm immediately with your <med>midwife</med>, <med>GP</med>, or <med>health visitor</med>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: New mother, 2–3 wk post-delivery  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
• Occasional, mild intrusive worries about infant safety (nocturnal breathing) – no panic attacks  
• Transient tearfulness when fatigued; denies persistent sadness, hopelessness, or crying spells  
• Denies anhedonia, sustained low mood, guilt, self-blame, or feeling overwhelmed  
• Denies sleep disruption beyond infant-related awakenings  
• Denies any self-harm ideation  

Pattern  
Episodic, situation-specific worry and brief fatigue-related tearfulness; otherwise euthymic and engaged.

Screening significance  
Current findings below conventional cut-offs for major postpartum depression; no evidence of moderate–severe anxiety or safety risk. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and psycho-education; re-screen if worsening mood, anxiety, or functioning.
